primary.thesis: The ladder's layout (the nearest upside strikes are $100-110, the nearest downside strikes are $80-85, and the upside runs out to $200) suggests front-month WTI was trading at roughly $90-95 on 2026-03-30. That level only makes sense after a Gulf supply shock that added a large risk premium. My view is that the extreme tails do not print on a front-month settlement by the last trading day of June. Two things drive this. First, a $150+ settlement would need a physical outage that is both sustained and large, on the scale of a months-long Hormuz closure, with no offset. The offsets are real: SPR and IEA coordinated stock releases, spare capacity routed through the Saudi East-West and UAE Habshan-Fujairah pipelines, US shale response, and demand destruction, which bites hard above about $120. Second, the resolution rules count only official daily settlements, not intraday spikes. Front-month rolls happen two business days before expiry, which removes most of the tail from a thin, squeezed expiring contract. On the downside, falling from a shock-level price to $40 inside three months would take both a full de-escalation and a demand collapse on the scale of a recession. That is a large move even on a quick ceasefire, because inventories drawn down during the shock have to be rebuilt.

basket.reason: $200 is more than double the implied level, with no historical precedent for a front-month settlement. Demand destruction and policy response cap the price well below it.
$175 needs a sustained, unmitigated loss of millions of barrels per day that lasts through June settlements. Only settlement prices count, not intraday spikes.
$150 would beat the 2008 nominal record on a settlement basis. Stock releases, pipeline bypasses and demand rationing make that hard to hold for even one daily settle.
From a shock-level price, reaching $40 by June needs de-escalation plus a demand collapse plus an OPEC+ price war, all inside a single quarter. Restocking after the shock supports the price floor.

failure_narrative: The upside legs lose if the Strait of Hormuz is effectively closed for weeks, or Gulf export infrastructure (Abqaiq, Ras Tanura, Qatari or Emirati terminals) is physically damaged. Tanker insurance withdrawal would also strand the bypass pipelines' capacity. Strategic stock releases would then prove too small and too slow. Front-month WTI could then settle at $150 or more on at least one day, most likely near a contract expiry when physical buyers scramble for prompt barrels at Cushing. The $40 NO leg loses in the opposite world: a sudden comprehensive settlement reopens flows, OPEC+ floods the market to regain share, and a global recession, possibly triggered by the shock itself, collapses demand. A disorderly unwind of speculative length then pushes front-month settlements below $40 by late June.
hedge_thesis: The main way the basket loses is a physical Gulf export outage that drives WTI to $150 or more. In exactly those worlds, seaborne LNG from the same chokepoint, above all Qatar's Ras Laffan volumes that pass through Hormuz, is also disrupted. European (TTF) and Asian (JKM) gas prices would then spike far beyond their normal levels. Europe and North-East Asia (Japan, Korea, Taiwan) would compete for Atlantic cargoes, and the result would be power-price spikes, emergency storage measures and industrial demand curtailment in Europe. The mechanism is a shared chokepoint and shared shipping and insurance risk. The same event that removes crude barrels removes roughly a fifth of global LNG supply, and gas markets have far less spare capacity and strategic storage to absorb it than oil does. So gas-price instruments pay off when oil touches the extreme high strikes.
